newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Unprecedented Irish give-away budget seen.
newsitem.headline: Unprecedented Irish give-away budget seen.

text.p: A leading Irish economist said on Tuesday that Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn's election year budget on Wednesday would give unprecedented personal tax cuts "so that every one comes out of it with a smile."

Jim O'Leary, chief economist with Davy Stockbrokers, said that Quinn, cashing in on strong economic growth and brimming government coffers, would introduce a give-away budget, with few precedents in Irish economic history.
"There is no question that this budget, in the league of give-away budgets, will be top," O'Leary told Irish radio 24 hours before Quinn delivers the budget in parliament.

He and other economists expect the government to spend up to 400 million punts ($654.6 million) cutting taxes, with up to two percentage points being shaved off standard income tax, currently 27 percent, and a cut in pay-related social insurance.

Their main concern is that the handouts might fuel a consumer boom which would push up inflation and tarnish Ireland's otherwise glowing credentials to be among the first members of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Quinn is expected to restate Ireland's determination to join the project and to boast that government finances are closer to meeting the European Union's Maastricht criteria for joining EMU than most of its bigger and wealthier rivals.
But the Irish Central Bank is reported to be concerned that too much cash in the hands of consumers might fuel inflation and necessitate an interest rate rise in 1997.
Maastricht guidelines states that inflation must not exceed that of the three best-performing EU states by more than 1.5 percent but that members must keep a stable and credible exchange rate.
Ireland's 1996 current budget was 292 million pounds in surplus against an expected deficit of 82 million punts and government finances have not been in better shape for 20 years.
It may be Quinn's last budget before the three-party right-left coalition of Prime Minister John Bruton fights an election, which is due by November.
But most political analysts expect him to call the election in the glow of a give-away budget, probably in May.
O'Leary said that previous budgets have eased Ireland's tax burden mainly on the lowest paid but that Quinn's package would be an across the board tax cut to woo all voters.
"It is shaping up to be a very political budget. This budget...is going to deliver a much more even distribution of benefits and everyone is going to come out with a smile."
By his estimates, consumers could be as much as five percent better off by the time Quinn sits down at the end of his speech to fend off attacks from the opposition Fianna Fail party and its allies.
They are expected to accuse Quinn of squandering the nation's wealth and of failing to control public spending.
